prompt: Why is SQLite a poor target for practicing the kind of external-contribution process this module teaches, despite being enormously widely deployed?
choices: It has too few real-world users to matter
Its maintainers deliberately do not accept external code contributions, citing the public-domain provenance of the code and testing burden
It requires a paid contributor license before any patch is considered
It is written in a language too obscure for most contributors to read

prompt: Where does substantive design discussion and review for a PostgreSQL patch actually happen?
choices: In comments on the postgres/postgres GitHub mirror
On the pgsql-hackers mailing list, with patch status tracked through the CommitFest app
In a private Slack channel restricted to committers
In Trac tickets, the same system Django uses

prompt: Roughly how long did PostgreSQL's MERGE command take to go from first proposal to being committed, and what was the core technical issue that kept stalling it?
choices: About 2 years, stalled over disagreement on SQL-standard syntax
About 13 years, stalled repeatedly over how MERGE's per-row actions interact with MVCC and concurrent updates
About 6 months, stalled purely from lack of committer interest
About 5 years, stalled over a licensing dispute

prompt: Django's DEP 0009 (async support), championed by Andrew Godwin, is a useful example mainly because of which characteristic of how it landed?
choices: It was implemented in full as a single massive pull request in one release
The Technical Board rejected it outright and it was never implemented
It was deliberately phased across multiple releases: ASGI handling first, then async views and middleware, then incremental async ORM support
It bypassed Django's design-review process entirely because Godwin held special authority

prompt: A contributor opens a 900-line PR against SQLAlchemy adding a new bulk-insert API with no prior issue or discussion, and Mike Bayer closes it saying to discuss the design first. What does this illustrate?
choices: SQLAlchemy rejects all contributions from people outside its core team on principle
Substantive design changes need discussion and buy-in before implementation — writing the code first is often the wrong order of operations, even for skilled contributors
The PR was closed only because it exceeded a hard 500-line limit
SQLAlchemy only accepts contributions from paid contractors

prompt: What structurally distinguishes a genuinely non-trivial contribution (to Django, SQLAlchemy, or PostgreSQL) from a typo-fix PR?
choices: Only the number of lines changed — anything over 50 lines counts as non-trivial
Whether the change happens to touch a test file

A non-trivial change involves a stated problem, discussion of alternatives and backward compatibility, an implementation meeting the project's test/doc bar, and typically several review rounds that can span months
Whether the change was written in a statically typed language

prompt: In PostgreSQL's CommitFest workflow, what does a patch status of "Returned with Feedback" mean?
choices: The patch is permanently rejected and cannot ever be resubmitted
The patch was committed but still needs a documentation follow-up
The patch isn't ready to be committed in this cycle and is sent back to the author, who can improve it and resubmit in a future CommitFest
The patch has been auto-merged pending a committer's final sign-off

prompt: Compared to the open-source contribution work covered in Tier 3, what makes projects like Django's core, SQLAlchemy, and PostgreSQL a meaningfully higher bar for this tier?
choices: They are written in a different programming language than the Tier 3 projects
They have real governance, high correctness and compatibility stakes, and require navigating an actual design-review process rather than picking up a labeled starter issue
They no longer use git for version control
They do not accept any external contributions, so the work is purely observational
